intro.why: Many words have several meanings, and applications (search, translation, question answering, knowledge-graph building) must pick the right one. Lexical resources like WordNet and the classic WSD methods show how meaning can be organised and chosen from context; the same ideas reappear in embedding-based retrieval.

sections.title: Lexemes, lemmas and senses
sections.plain: A dictionary entry, its citation form, and each of its distinct meanings.
sections.body:
"I went to the bank." Which bank? Add "to withdraw money" or "and watched the ducks" and the meaning is obvious. Nothing about the word changed; the context did: word + context = meaning (a word is known by the company it keeps, which is why bidirectional models like BERT read both sides).

  • Lexeme: the abstract dictionary entry, a family of word forms.
  • Lemma: its canonical citation form, to which all forms map: run for runs/ran/running; carpet for carpets. Lemmatisation (M1) walks from forms to lemmas.
  • Sense: one particular meaning of a lexeme: bank₁ = financial institution, bank₂ = sloping land beside a river.

Lemmatisation groups forms; it does not choose a sense. That is the job of word sense disambiguation.

sections.title: Homonymy vs polysemy
sections.plain: Same spelling with unrelated meanings, versus one word with related meanings.
sections.body:
Homonymy: identical form, unrelated meanings. "The bat is heavy to hold" (cricket bat) vs "A bat is hanging on the tree" (mammal); "the cricket match" vs "a good match for him". Two strangers who happen to share a name.

Polysemy: related meanings sharing a core idea. Paper: research paper, question paper, newspaper, gift-wrap paper (all still paper); mouth of a person, a river, a cave (an opening). One person wearing different hats.

homonymypolysemy
meaningsunrelatedrelated, one core idea
examplebat (animal / cricket bat)paper (news / question / wrapping)
dictionaryusually separate entriesone entry, numbered senses

The test is a single question: are the meanings related to one core idea?

sections.title: Synonymy, antonymy, hypernymy and meronymy
sections.plain: Words relate as near-equals, opposites, general–specific pairs, and part–whole pairs.
sections.body:
• Synonyms: (nearly) the same meaning: big/large, angry/mad/furious. Perfect synonyms are rare: an elder sibling is your big brother, never your large brother.
  • Antonyms: opposites: hot/cold, rich/poor, open/close.
  • Hypernym / hyponym: parent (more general) / child (more specific): vehicle → car → SUV; animal → dog → golden retriever. The same node can be both: car is a hyponym of vehicle and a hypernym of SUV. Chaining these links grows a hierarchy.
  • Meronym / holonym: part / whole: wheel and steering wheel are parts of a car; fingers are part of a hand. It answers "what is this a piece of?" rather than "what kind of thing is this?".

sections.title: Synsets and relations by part of speech
sections.plain: Group synonyms into one concept node, and use relation types that fit each part of speech.
sections.body:
A synset (synonym set) is a group of words expressing one concept, e.g. {intelligent, clever, bright, brilliant, smart}. In WordNet the node is the synset, and words are labels on it; one spelling can label several synsets.

Relations are organised by part of speech:

  • Nouns: hypernymy/hyponymy (vehicle/car), meronymy/holonymy (wheel/car).
  • Verbs: hierarchies too: move is a hypernym of walk; sleep of snore (snoring is a particular way of sleeping: troponymy); entailment (snoring entails sleeping; buying entails paying).
  • Adjectives: antonymy (hot/cold) and similarity clusters (hot ~ warm, scorching).

sections.title: WordNet as a lexical graph
sections.plain: A dictionary rewired as a network of concepts, where position tells you meaning.
sections.body:
WordNet is a lexical database: the dictionary stored as a graph, organised by meaning rather than alphabetically. Every synset is a node; every relation (hypernym, meronym, antonym…) an edge. It looks like a forest of hierarchies under top concepts (entity → living things, artifacts…) tied together by cross-links.

"bat" appears in two neighbourhoods: bat₁ under mammal → animal → entity, bat₂ under sports equipment → artifact → entity. Once a system knows which node a sentence means, it inherits everything above it: bat₁ is a mammal, hence an animal, without anyone writing that down.

  • Meaning by position: what a node connects to tells you what it means.
  • Inheritance for free: properties flow down parent–child chains.
  • Similarity: path similarity = 1/(1 + path length through the lowest common ancestor): bat₁–dog = 1/3 (siblings under mammal), bat₁–bat₂ = 1/7 (only entity in common).
  • A map for disambiguation: an ambiguous word points at several nodes; context decides which.

sections.title: The most-frequent-sense baseline
sections.plain: With no clues, guess the sense that's most common overall.
sections.body:
WSD decides, for an ambiguous word in a particular sentence, which sense is intended, like answering a multiple-choice question with the senses as options. Four families of methods follow, from crudest to most modern.

Most frequent sense (MFS): if 80% of uses of "bat" in a sense-tagged corpus mean the cricket bat, always guess that: right 80% of the time with no context at all. It is a strong baseline that every cleverer method must beat, yet it fails exactly where the rare sense appears ("the bat flew out of the cave") and degrades when the test domain's sense distribution differs from training (a wildlife documentary).

sections.title: Naive Bayes disambiguation
sections.plain: Learn from labelled sentences which context words go with which sense, and multiply the evidence.
sections.body:
Supervised WSD trains a classifier on sentences whose target word has been sense-tagged by hand. Naive Bayes assumes context words are independent given the sense:

$$P(s\mid w_1,\dots,w_n) \propto P(s)\prod_i P(w_i\mid s),\qquad P(w\mid s) = \frac{\text{count}(w, s) + 1}{\text{total}(s) + V}$$

Worked: "The bank approved my loan". 8 finance and 2 river training sentences → P(fin) = 0.8, P(riv) = 0.2. Context vocabulary V = 6 {loan, approved, money, water, fishing, river}; finance counts 4, 2, 3, 0, 0, 1 (total 10); river 0, 0, 0, 2, 1, 2 (total 5).

  • P(loan | fin) = 5/16 = 0.3125; P(approved | fin) = 3/16 = 0.1875 → score 0.8 × 0.3125 × 0.1875 = 0.0469.
  • P(loan | riv) = P(approved | riv) = 1/11 = 0.0909 → 0.2 × 0.0909 × 0.0909 = 0.0017.

Finance wins by ~28×; smoothing kept the river sense off a hard zero. The independence assumption suits bag-of-context-words reasonably well; with correlated numeric features (two features derived from the same source data) it can badly mislead, so check correlations before trusting it. Labelled data is the bottleneck: it is expensive per word.

sections.title: Embedding-similarity disambiguation
sections.plain: Embed the sentence and each sense's definition; choose the closest.
sections.body:
Sentence encoders (from roughly 2016–17 onward) embed any text, a word, a sentence or a document, as a vector. WSD becomes geometry:

  1. Embed the sentence containing the ambiguous word → s.
  2. Embed each candidate sense's gloss → m₁, m₂, ….
  3. Choose the sense with the highest cosine (or dot product) with s.

"The bank approved my loan" lands close to "financial institution that lends money" (cosine ≈ 0.98 in the toy example) and far from "sloping land beside a river" (≈ 0.49). No hand-written rules and no sense-labelled training set; contextual embeddings (BERT) sharpen this further because the vector for "bank" itself shifts with its neighbours. This is the modern default, and the same machinery powers semantic search and retrieval (M14).

sections.title: The Lesk algorithm and comparing methods
sections.plain: Pick the sense whose dictionary definition shares the most words with the sentence.
sections.body:
Lesk works like a recruiter shortlisting by keyword overlap: the sentence is the job description, each gloss a résumé, and the sense with most overlapping words wins. "The bank approved my loan": context {approved, loan}; finance gloss "a financial institution that accepts deposits and provides loans and mortgages" overlaps 1 (loan ~ loans after normalisation); river gloss "sloping land beside a body of water, the shore of a river" overlaps 0 → finance.

Weakness: exact matching is brittle. "The fisherman caught a bass": neither the fish gloss (fish, sea, water) nor the music gloss (music, guitar, band) contains "fisherman": 0 vs 0. Fixes: stemming or prefix matching (fisherman ~ fish), extended Lesk (also use glosses of related synsets), richer glosses such as encyclopedia pages and their links, or embedding similarity. WordNet also allows a structural route: check whether the context talks about the mammal or the sports-equipment neighbourhood.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Sense granularity: WordNet distinguishes very fine senses; even human annotators agree only ~70–80% at that level, so coarse sense groups are often used.
  • Evaluation: SemCor and SensEval/SemEval datasets; report accuracy against the MFS baseline.
  • Implicit WSD: modern LLMs and translation models disambiguate internally; explicit WSD remains useful for linking text to lexicons and knowledge graphs.
  • One sense per discourse: a word tends to keep one sense throughout a document, a useful heuristic.

code.title: A mini WordNet
code.explain: Builds a small synset graph with hypernym links, finds both senses of 'bat' and their chains (mammal → animal vs sports equipment → artifact), shows car as both hyponym and hypernym, meronyms and antonyms, and computes path similarity (bat₁–dog 0.333, bat₁–bat₂ 0.143, car–SUV 0.5).
mistakes: Treating a spelling as a single node.
code.notes: NLTK's WordNet interface offers the same operations on the full database.
